Findings:- 

6. Point No.I:-As per claim statement, Petitioner alleges that he joined the service of the Respondent Food 
Corporation of India as Male casual labour on 4.1.1996 and he worked for more than 4 to 5 years continuously 
without any break. Petitioner submits that he has completed more than 240 days in a calendar year hence, he is 
entitled to notice, notice pay before termination from the employment. However, Respondent did not issue any 
notice nor paid any wages in lieu of notice as compensation under Section 25F of ID Act and Respondent has 
terminated Petitioner from service in violation of the provision contained under section 25 F of ID Act. Further 
alleged that termination order of Petitioner is illegal and he is entitled to reinstatement in the service with all 
consequential benefits. Further, Petitioner submits that Supreme Court in catena of decisions has held that temporary 
employee cannot be replaced by another temporary employee. In the instant matter all the workers have been 
disengaged by engaging fresh workmen as telegraphic messengers by the Respondent in violation of section 25G 
and 25H of I.D. Act, 1947. Petitioner prayed to set aside his termination order dated 10.12.2002 and to reinstate 
him into service. 


7. का support of claim Petitioner, has filed chief statement affidavit of WW1 and WW1 in his affidavit has 
reiterated the averments made in the claim statement, WW1 states that his service has been terminated by oral order 
on 10.12.2002 by the Respondent in contravention of the provision of Section 25 F of the I.D. Act. Petitioner has also 
filed photocopies of ten documents in evidence 1.6. Ex.W1 to W10. Ex.W1, W2, W3 and W8, these documents 
include representations dated 22.1.1996, 25.9.1997, 5.12.1998 and 12.8.2004 to the Respondent management to issue 
identity card. Ex.W4 is the letter of Asst. Manager, FCI, Hanuman Junction dated 21.8.99 extending duties of 
petitioner for watch and ward. Ex.W5 is the conduct certificate issued by Respondent stating therein that Petitioner 
workman was working as a casual labour on piece rate basis and his behavior and good conduct has been certified. 
Ex.W6 and W7 are identity cards. Ex.W9 is the order passed in WP No.1112/2006 whereby petitioner along with 
other workers has withdrawn his writ petition filed before Hon'ble High Court. Ex.W10 is the legal notice issued by 
counsel for petitioner to Respondent dated 16.07.2007. WWI was not cross examined by the Respondent, however 
Respondent did not adduce any evidence. 


8. It is settled law that initial burden of proof to establish retrenchment in violation of provision of Section 
25 F of ID Act lies on petitioner. Petitioner has to prove by evidence that he has been in service of Respondent for 
240 days continuously in a calendar year just preceding from the date of his termination. 


Before appreciation of evidence on record, it would be apposite to have a glance of the relevant provision contained 
under ID Act and same is reproduced hereunder: - 


Section 25B defines the term continuous service which provides 
Definition of continuous service.- For the purposes of this Chapter, -- 


(1) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in uninterrupted 
service, including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or authorized leave or an accident 
or a Strike which is not illegal, or a lock- out or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of 
the workman; 

(2) where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (1) for a period of one year or 
six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer-- 

(a) for a period of one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with 
reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the employer for not less than-- 

(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below ground in a mine; and 


(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : सितम्बर 27, 2025/आश्विन 5, 1947 6287 


Section 25 F provides: - 
25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen. 


- No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an 
employer shall be retrenched by that employer until- 


(a) the workman has been given one month 's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the 
period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the 
notice. 


(b)the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen 
days ‘average pay [for every completed year of continuous service] [ Substituted by Act 36 of 1964, Section 14, 
for " for every completed year of service" (w.e.f. 19.12.1964).] or any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c)notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government [or such authority as may be 
specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette. ] 


Further, Hon'ble Supreme Court in its various decisions has explained the concept of continuous service in a 
calendar year u/s 25F of I.D Act. some of the relevant decisions are discussed here under:- 


In the case of Sur Enamel and Stamping works Private Limited Vs. their workmen, referring to Section 
25 8, Hon'ble Supreme Court has defined the term continuous service as under: - 


"The position therefore is that during a period of employment for less than 11 calendar months these two 
persons worked for more than 240 days. In our opinion that would not satisfy the requirement of section 25B. 
Before a workman can be considered to have completed one year of continuous service in an industry it must be 
shown first that he was employed for a period of not less than 12 calendar months and, next that during those 
12 calendar months had worked for not less than 240 days. Where, as in the present case, the workmen have not 
at all been employed for a period of 12 calendar months it becomes unnecessary to examine whether the actual 
days of work numbered 240 days or more. For, in any case, the requirements of section 25B would not be 
satisfied by the mere fact of the number of working days being not less than 240 days." 


In Mohan Lal Vs. Management of M/s. Bharat Electronics, dated 21.4.1981AIR 1981 Supreme Court 1253, the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court have held, 


It was, however, urged that section 25F is not attracted in this case for an entirely different reason. Mr. 
Markendaya contended that before section 25F is invoked, the condition of eligibility for a workman to 
complain of invalid retrenchment must be satisfied. According to him unless the workman has put in continuous 
service for not less than one year his case would not be governed by section 25F. That is substantially correct 
because the relevant provision of section 25F provides as under: 


"25F. "No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year 
under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until: - 


(a) the workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the 
period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the 
notice; 


Provided that no such notice shall be necessary if the retrenchment is under an agreement which specifies a 
date for the termination of service; 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent of fifteen 
days' average pay (for every completed year of continuous service) or any part thereof in excess of six months; 
and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government (or such authority as may be 
specified by the appropriate government by notification in the Official Gazette)." 


Reverting to the facts of this case, admittedly the appellant was employed and was on duty from December 8, 
1973 to October 19, 1974 when his service was terminated. The relevant date will be the date of termination of 
service, t.e. October 19, 1974 Commencing from that date and counting backwards, admittedly he had rendered 
service for a period of 240 days within a period of 12 months and, indisputably, therefore, his case falls within 
section 25B(2) (a) and he shall be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose 
of Chapter VA.” 


In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim was 
denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in the year 
preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor and that cannot be 


6288 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA :SEPTEMBER 27, 2025/ASVINA 5, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in fact the claimant had 
worked for 240 days in a year These aspects were highlighted in Range Forest Officer v. S.T. Hadimani (2002 (3) 
SCC 25. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record in that regard was produced. Mere 
non-production of the muster roll for a particular period was not sufficient for the Labour Court held that the 
workman had worked for 240 days as claimed." 


In Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas (2004 (8) SCC 195), held "the burden was on the workman to 
show that he was working for more than 240 days in the preceding one year prior to his alleged retrenchment." In 
MP. Electricity Board v. Hariram (2004 (8) SCC 246) the position was again reiterated in paragraph I1 as follows: 
"The above burden having not been discharged and the Labour Court having held so, in our opinion, the Industrial 
Court and the High Court erred in basing an order of reinstatement solely on an adverse inference drawn 
erroneously ..” 


In the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S Mani (2005) SCC Page 100, the 3 Judges Bench of the Apex 
Court held that "the initial burden of proof was on the workman to show that he had completed 240 days of service." 


In the case of Mohan Lal vs. Management, BEL 1981 SCC P. 225, Hon'ble Apex Court held, "Before a 
workman can claim retrenchment, not being in consonance of Section 25 of the ID act. he has to show that he has 
been in continuous service of not less than I year with the employer who had retrenched him from service." 


Now, in view of the provision contained under Section 25B of I D Act and Law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court as discussed above, we have to examine whether retrenchment of petitioner workman by Respondent vide 
oral order dated 10.12.2002 is in contravention of the provision contained under section 25F. As per provision 
contained under Section 25 B of the I.D. Act, 1947, the petitioner workman has to prove the fact of continuous 
service of 240 days in a calendar year just preceding from the date of termination i.e.,10.12.2002 by leading 
documentary as well as oral evidence. As claimed by Petitioner he was terminated by oral order on 10.12.2002. 
The record goes to reveals that Petitioner has not filed any document in evidence to establish the fact that he had 
rendered continuous service for a period of 240 days in the Respondent office in a calendar year just preceding from 
the date of his termination i.e.,10.12.2002., Petitioner has not filed any document of salary slips or wage payment 
slips or attendance register or appointment letter or certificate in order to prove that he has been engaged by 
Respondent for work during the period of 240 days just preceding for date of termination i.e. 10.12.2002. Thus, 
Petitioner failed to prove that he had worked 240 days continuously in a calendar year just preceding from the date 
of his termination. However, Respondent has averred in counter that identity card issued by the Asst. 
Manager(Depot) is useful to show at the gate point only for entry into depot. The corporation will issue identity card 
with emblem in the prescribed form duly signed by the Area Manager only, for the regular employees. In fact, the 
corporation introduced Direct Payment System to the casual labour in the year 1997, itself. Under this system, the 
registers were maintained. The said register did not disclose the name of the Petitioner as casual labour. Hence, this 
contention of the Petitioner is not supported by valid proof. However, Petitioner has not rebutted or contradicted 
contention of Respondent by producing any cogent evidence. However, said Identity card filed by the petitioner in 
evidence pertains to the year 1997-1999 and do not pertain to year 2002 when the petitioner was terminated. 
Therefore, the Identity card filed by Petitioner have no relevance to establish fact of continuous service as required u/s 
25-F of ID Act. 


10. Thus, ongoing documentary and oral evidence on record, I am of the view that Petitioner has utterly 
failed to establish that he had worked for 240 days continuously in a calendar year just preceding from the date of his 
termination i.e.,10.12.2002 . Therefore, provision of Sec.25F of I.D. Act, 1947 do not apply to his case. Thus, for 
the want of evidence, the claim of petitioner that he has completed 240 days of continuous service in a calendar year 
just preceding from the date of his termination i.e.,10.12.2002 is not tenable. Thus Petitioner failed to establish and 
prove that his retrenchment is illegal in contravention of provision u/s.25F of I.D. Act, 1947, and the claim of the 
Petitioner for reinstatement in the employment of Respondent u/s 250 and 25H is not tenable. 


Thus, Issue No.I is answered against the Petitioner. 


13. Issue No.II:- As per record, undisputedly, Petitioner has not filed any appointment letter of his employment in 
evidence. It is admitted fact that Respondent used to take the work from him as and when required. Thus, it is 
established that Petitioner had worked as causal labour in Respondent management. Respondent in his counter has 
submitted that the Petitioner was never engaged as casual labour at any point of time, hence, no question of 
terminating his from services arise. There was no employer and employee relationship between the Petitioner and the 
Respondent. Respondent in counter has contended that management being instrumentality of the Government, bound 
by rules and regulations for recruitment of employees for the organization. 


As regard claim of petitioner for regularization in the service, Hon'ble Supreme Court in its recent decision has laid 
down principles and guidelines for regularization of casual workman, In the case of ONGC Vs. Krishan Gopal 
2020(3) Scale 272,Hon'ble Supreme Court of India have laid down the principle regarding regularization of 
the casual workman and have held:- 


“23 The following propositions would emerge upon analyzing the above decisions: 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : सितम्बर 27, 2025/आश्विन 5, 1947 6289 


(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to 
order regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions 
contained in Article 14 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status 
of permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour 
practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ 
workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on 
lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years 
of service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be 
open to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been 
regularised to make a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit 
would amount to a violation of Article 14; and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 10 of the Vth Schedule of 
the ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them 
for years, with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen.” 


But in the instant matter, Petitioner has failed to adduce any evidence that he was appointed by Respondent by 
following recruitment procedure or he was working against any sanctioned permanent post in the Respondent 
management. Petitioner failed to adduce any evidence on record that the Respondent was indulged in any unfair 
labour practice by not filling the permanent post even though such post was available and by calling to employ 
workman as temporary or daily wages employees despite performing the same work as regular workman on lower 
wages. Therefore, for the want of such plea and evidence, the claim of the Petitioner for regularization in the 
Respondent service is not acceptable. 


Further, in the case of Hari Nandan Prasad v Employer I/R to Management of Food Corporation of India20 
(“FCI”), Hon'ble Supreme Court of India have held: 


“34. On a harmonious reading of the two judgments discussed in detail above, we are of the opinion that when 
there are posts available, in the absence of any unfair labour practice the Labour Court would not give 
direction for regularisation only because a worker has continued as daily- wage worker/ad hoc/temporary 
worker for number of years. Further, if there are no posts available, such a direction for regularization would 
be impermissible. In the aforesaid circumstances giving of direction to regularise such a person, only on the 
basis of number of years put in by such a worker as daily-wager, etc. may amount to back door entry into the 
service which is an anathema to Article 14 of the Constitution. Further, such a direction would not be given 
when the worker concerned does not meet the eligibility requirement of the post in question as per the 
recruitment rules. However, wherever it is found that similarly situated workmen are regularised by the 
employer itself under some scheme or otherwise and the workmen in question who have approached the 
Industrial/Labour Court are on a par with them, direction of regularisation in such cases may be legally 
justified, otherwise, non-regularisation of the left-over workers itself would amount to invidious discrimination 
qua them in such cases and would be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Thus, the industrial adjudicator 
would be achieving the equality by upholding Article 14, rather than violating this constitutional provision.” 


Thus, in view of the fore gone discussion and law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above, the 
claim of the Petitioner for regularization is not tenable. 


Thus, Point No.II is decided against the Petitioner accordingly. 


14. Point No.l: In view of the finding given at Points No. I & II, the Petitioner is not entitled to any relief 
claimed and his petition is found to be baseless, devoid of merit and hence, liable to be dismissed. 


Therefore, Point No.III is decided accordingly. 
AWARD 


The claim of the petitioner Shri Ch. Syam Kumar to set aside his termination order w.e.f 10-12-2002 by 
Respondent Management of Food Corporation of India, Hanuman Junction is dismissed. Petition sans merit, stands 
dismissed.

AWARD 


Sri U. Sambasiva Rao who worked as casual labour (who will be referred to as the workman) has filed this 
petition under Sec. 2A(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 against the Respondent s Food Corporation of India 
seeking for declaring the oral termination order dated 10.12.2002 issued by Respondent as illegal, arbitrary and to 
set aside the same consequently directing the Respondent s to reinstate the Petitioner into service duly granting all the 
consequential benefits such as continuity of service, back wages and all other attendant benefits etc., and such other 
reliefs as this court may deems fit. 


2. The averments made in the petition in brief are as follows: 


The Petitioner workman submits that he was engaged by the management as a Male Casual Labourer in the Food 
Corporation of India at Hanuman Junction on 06.03.1995, and worked as Office Boy, also performing additional 
duties as Storesman and Watchman under the control of the third Respondent . He was drawing a salary of Rs. 1500/- 
p.m., at the time his termination. He worked continuously without any break in service. As per the management’s 
procedure, he submitted applications dated 17.9.1995, 6.12.1998 and 19.9.1997 to the second and third Respondent s 
for issuance of Identification Cards, which were issued accordingly. The second Respondent, through proceedings 
No. FCI/BSC/Hanuman Junction/S&C/1990-2000 dated 21.08.1999, confirmed the workman’s employment and 
joining date as 06.03.1995. The workman submits that the nature of his duties was permanent and he completed more 
than 240 days of service each year. The third Respondent issued a Conduct Certificate confirming his service as Male 
Casual Labourer. The claimant submitted a representation dated 06.12.1997 to the third Respondent for 
regularization. Based on this, the Assistant Manager (Depot) addressed a letter dated 19.12.1997 to the second 
Respondent , stating that the claimant worked as Gardener, handled maintenance work, and recommended 
regularization. However, no action was taken. Another representation dated 20.09.1998 was also made, but the 
management failed to respond. It is submitted that on 10.12.2002, while discharging his duties, the second and third 
Respondent s came to the Buffer Storage Complex, Hanuman Junction, and orally informed the claimant that his 
services were not required, and sent him away, thereby terminating him from service. The termination, instead of 
regularization, was oral, illegal, arbitrary, and in violation of Section 25(F) of the I.D. Act, as no one-month notice, 
pay in lieu thereof, or compensation was given, making the termination void ab initio and liable to be set aside. After 
termination, the claimant made several requests for reinstatement, including a representation to the first Respondent 
on 21.08.2004, but without success. The claimant got issued a legal notice dated 13.07.2004 to the second Respondent 
seeking reinstatement, but there was no response. It is submitted that workman also issued a legal notice dated 
16.07.2007 to the first and second Respondent s requesting reinstatement. Despite receipt, no reply was given by 
either Respondent . The claimant submits he has been making representations to the management stating he worked 
from 1995 to 2001 without any break in service, in the posts of Office Boy, Storesman, and Watchman, which are

permanent posts. Instead of regularizing his services, the management terminated him and engaged persons junior to 
him. The act of engaging new casual labour ignoring the candidature of the claimant is illegal, arbitrary, and against

Labour and sought regularization. | However, no action was taken, despite the claimant being senior. The

The Respondent s never promised employment to the Petitioner. They are not responsible for his unemployment. 
Though he alleges oral termination on 10.12.2002, his inaction thereafter disproves the claim. The ID is barred by 
limitation and is liable to be dismissed. It is therefore prayed that the claim petition be dismissed. 


4. | Heard arguments of Learned Counsel for Petitioner and perused written arguments filed by Petitioner. 


5. | On the basis of rival contentions and _ pleadings of both the parties, following issues emerge for 
determination in the instant matter:- 


I. Whether the action of Respondent Management Food Corporation of India, Hanuman Junction in orally 
terminating the services of Petitioner Sri U. Sambasiva Rao with effect from 10.12.2002 is legal and 
justified? 

Il. Whether the Petitioner is entitled for regularization? 


Ill. Whether the Petitioner is entitled for the relief claimed? 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : सितम्बर 27, 2025/आश्विन 5, 1947 6293 


Findings:- 


6. Point No.I:-As per claim statement, Petitioner alleges that he joined the service of the Respondent Food 
Corporation of India as Male casual labour on 6.3.1995 and he worked for more than 4 to 5 years continuously 
without any break. Petitioner submits that he has completed more than 240 days in a calendar year hence, he is 
entitled to notice, notice pay before termination from the employment. However, Respondent did not issue any 
notice nor paid any wages in lieu of notice as compensation under Section 25F of ID Act and Respondent has 
terminated Petitioner from service in violation of the provision contained under section 25 F of ID Act. Further 
alleged that termination order of Petitioner is illegal and he is entitled to reinstatement in the service with all 
consequential benefits. Further, Petitioner submits that Supreme Court in catena of decisions has held that temporary 
employee cannot be replaced by another temporary employee. In the instant matter all the workers have been 
disengaged by engaging fresh workmen as telegraphic messengers by the Respondent in violation of section 25G 
and 25H of I.D. Act, 1947. Petitioner prayed to set aside his termination order dated 10.12.2002 and to reinstate 
him into service. 


7. In support of claim Petitioner, has filed chief statement affidavit of WW1 and WW1 in his affidavit has 
reiterated the averments made in the claim statement, WW1 states that his service has been terminated by oral order 
on 10.12.2002 by the Respondent in contravention of the provision of Section 25 F of the I.D. Act. Petitioner has also 
filed photocopies of eleven documents in evidence i.e. Ex.W1, W2, W3 and W5. These documents includes 
representations dated 17.3.1995, 19.9.1997, 16.12.1998 and 16.12.1997 to the Respondent management to issue 
identity card. Ex.W4 is the letter of Asst. Manager, FCI, Hanuman Junction dated 21.8.99 extending duties of 
petitioner for watch and ward. Ex.W6 is the conduct certificate issued by Respondent stating therein that Petitioner 
workman was working as a casual labour on piece rate basis from January ‘98 to June ’99 and his behavior and good 
conduct has been certified. Ex.W7 , W8 and W9 are identity cards. Ex.W10 is the order passed in WP No.1112/2006 
whereby petitioner along with other workers has withdrawn his writ petition filed before Hon'ble High Court. 
Ex.W11 is the legal notice issued by counsel for petitioner to Respondent dated 16.07.2007. WW1 was not cross 
examined by the Respondent, however Respondent did not adduce any evidence. 


8. It is settled law that initial burden of proof to establish retrenchment in violation of provision of Section 
25 F of ID Act lies on petitioner. Petitioner has to prove by evidence that he has been in service of Respondent for 
240 days continuously in a calendar year just preceding from the date of his termination. 


Before appreciation of evidence on record of Petitioner, it would be aposite to have a glance on the relevant provision 
contained under ID Act and same is reproduced hereunder:- 


Section 25B defines the term continuous service which provides 
Definition of continuous service.- For the purposes of this Chapter,-- 


(1) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in uninterrupted 
service, including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or authorized leave or an accident 
or a Strike which is not illegal, or a lock- out or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of 
the workman; 


(2) where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (1) for a period of one year or 
six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer-- 


(a) for a period of one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with 
reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the employer for not less than-- 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below ground in a mine; and 
(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 
Section 25 F provides: - 

25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen. 


- No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an 
employer shall be retrenched by that employer until- 


(a) the workman has been given one month 's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the 
period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the 
notice. 


(b)the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen 
days ‘average pay [for every completed year of continuous service] [ Substituted by Act 36 of 1964, Section 14, 
for " for every completed year of service" (w.e.f. 19.12.1964).] or any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


6294 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA :SEPTEMBER 27, 2025/ASVINA 5, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(c)notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government [or such authority as may be 
specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette. ] 


Further, Hon'ble Supreme Court in its various decisions has explained the concept of continuous service in a calendar 
year u/s 25F of I.D Act. some of the relevant decisions are discussed here under:- 


In the case of Sur Enamel and Stamping works Private Limited Vs. their workmen, referring to Section 25 B, 
Hon'ble Supreme Court has defined the term continuous service as under:- 


"The position therefore is that during a period of employment for less than 11 calendar months these two 
persons worked for more than 240 days. In our opinion that would not satisfy the requirement of section 25B. 
Before a workman can be considered to have completed one year of continuous service in an industry it must be 
shown first that he was employed for a period of not less than 12 calendar months and, next that during those 
12 calendar months had worked for not less than 240 days. Where, as in the present case, the workmen have not 
at all been employed for a period of 12 calendar months it becomes unnecessary to examine whether the actual 
days of work numbered 240 days or more. For, in any case, the requirements of section 25B would not be 
satisfied by the mere fact of the number of working days being not less than 240 days." 


In Mohan Lal Vs. Management of M/s. Bharat Electronics, dated 21.4.1981AIR 1981 Supreme Court 1253, the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court have held, 


It was, however, urged that section 25F is not attracted in this case for an entirely different reason. Mr. 
Markendaya contended that before section 25F is invoked, the condition of eligibility for a workman to 
complain of invalid retrenchment must be satisfied. According to him unless the workman has put in continuous 
service for not less than one year his case would not be governed by section 25F. That is substantially correct 
because the relevant provision of section 25F provides as under: 


"25F. "No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year 
under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until: - 


(a) the workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the 
period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the 
notice; 


Provided that no such notice shall be necessary if the retrenchment is under an agreement which specifies a 
date for the termination of service; 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent of fifteen 
days' average pay (for every completed year of continuous service) or any part thereof in excess of six months; 
and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government (or such authority as may be 
specified by the appropriate government by notification in the Official Gazette)." 


Reverting to the facts of this case, admittedly the appellant was employed and was on duty from December 8, 
1973 to October 19, 1974 when his service was terminated. The relevant date will be the date of termination of 
service, i.e. October 19, 1974 Commencing from that date and counting backwards, admittedly he had rendered 
service for a period of 240 days within a period of 12 months and, indisputably, therefore, his case falls within 
section 25B(2) (a) and he shall be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose 


of Chapter VA.” 
In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim 
was denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days 
in the year preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor 
and that cannot be regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in 
fact the claimant had worked for 240 days in a year These aspects were highlighted in Range Forest Officer v. 
S.T. Hadimani (2002 (3) SCC 25. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record in that 
regard was produced. Mere non-production of the muster roll for a particular period was not sufficient for the 
Labour Court held that the workman had worked for 240 days as claimed." 


In Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas (2004 (8) SCC 195), held "the burden was on the workman to 
show that he was working for more than 240 days in the preceding one year prior to his alleged retrenchment." In 
MP. Electricity Board v. Hariram (2004 (8) SCC 246) the position was again reiterated in paragraph I1 as follows: 
"The above burden having not been discharged and the Labour Court having held so, in our opinion, the Industrial 
Court and the High Court erred in basing an order of reinstatement solely on an adverse inference 
drawn erroneously ..” 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : सितम्बर 27, 2025/आश्विन 5, 1947 6295 


In the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S Mani (2005) SCC Page 100, the 3 Judges Bench of the Apex 
Court held that "the initial burden of proof was on the workman to show that he had completed 240 days of service." 


In the case of Mohan Lal vs. Management, BEL 1981 SCC P. 225, Hon'ble Apex Court held, "Before a 
workman can claim retrenchment, not being in consonance of Section 25 of the ID act. he has to show that he has 
been in continuous service of not less than I year with the employer who had retrenched him from service." 


Now, in view of the provision contained under Section 25B of I D Act and Law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court as discussed above, we have to examine whether retrenchment of petitioner workman by Respondent vide 
oral order dated 10.12.2002 is in contravention of the provision contained under section 25F. As per provision 
contained under Section 25 B of the I.D. Act, 1947, the petitioner workman has to prove the fact of continuous 
service of 240 days in a calendar year just preceding from the date of termination i.e.,10.12.2002 by leading 
documentary as well as oral evidence. As claimed by Petitioner he was terminated by oral order on 10.12.2002. 
The record goes to reveals that Petitioner has not filed any document in evidence to establish the fact that he had 
rendered continuous service for a period of 240 days in the Respondent office in a calendar year just preceding from 
the date of his termination i.e.,10.12.2002., Petitioner has not filed any document of salary slips or wage payment 
slips or attendance register or appointment letter or certificate in order to prove that he has been engaged by 
Respondent for worked during the period of 240 days just preceding for date of termination i.e. 10.12.2002. Thus, 
Petitioner failed to prove that he had worked 240 days continuously in a calendar year just preceding from the date 
of his termination. However, Respondent has averred in counter that identity card issued by the Asst. 
Manager(Depot) is useful to show at the gate point only for entry into depot. The corporation will issue identity card 
with emblem in the prescribed form duly signed by the Area Manager only, for the regular employees. In fact, the 
corporation introduced Direct Payment System to the casual labour in the year 1997, itself. Under this system, the 
registers were maintained. The said registered did not disclose the name of the Petitioner as casual labour. Hence, 
this contention of the Petitioner is not supported by valid proof. However, Petitioner has not rebutted or contradicted 
this contention of Respondent by producing any cogent evidence. However said Identity card filed by the petitioner 
in evidence pertains to the year 1997-1999 and do not pertain to year 2002 when petitioner was terminated. 
Therefore, the Identity card have no relevance to establish fact of continuous service as required u/s 25-F of ID Act. 


10. Thus, ongoing documentary and oral evidence on record, I am of the view that Petitioner has utterly 
failed to establish that he had worked for 240 days continuously in a calendar year just preceding from the date of his 
termination i.e.,10.12.2002 . Therefore, provision of Sec.25F of I.D. Act, 1947 do not apply to his case. Thus, for 
the want of evidence, the claime of petitioner that he has completed 240 days of continuous service in a calendar year 
just preceding from the date of his termination 1.e.,10.12.2002 is not tenable. Thus Petitioner failed to establish and 
prove his retrenchment is illegal in contravention of provision u/s.25F of ID. Act, 1947, and the claim of the 
Petitioner for reinstatement in the employment of Respondent u/s 25G and 25H is not tenable. 


Thus, Issue No.I is answered against the Petitioner. 


13. Issue No.II:-As per record, undisputedly, Petitioner has not filed any appointment letter of employment in 
evidence. It is admitted fact that Respondent used to take the work from him as and when required. Thus, it is 
established that Petitioner had worked as causal labour in Respondent management. Respondent in his counter has 
submitted that the Petitioner was never engaged as casual labour at any point of time, hence, no question of 
terminating his from services arise. There was no employer and employee relationship between the Petitioner and the 
Respondent. Respondent in counter has contended that management being instrumentality of the Government, bound 
by rules and regulations for recruitment of employees for the organization. 


As claim of petitioner for regularization in the service, Hon'ble Supreme Court in its recent decision has laid down 
principles and guidelines for regularization of casual workman, In the case of ONGC Vs. Krishan Gopal 2020(3) 
Scale 272,Hon'ble Supreme Court of India have laid down the principle regarding regularization of the casual 
workman and have held:- 


“23 The following propositions would emerge upon analyzing the above decisions: 


(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to 
order regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions 
contained in Article 14 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status 
of permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour 
practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ 
workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on 
lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years 
of service; 


6296 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA :SEPTEMBER 27, 2025/ASVINA 5, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be 
open to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been 
regularised to make a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit 
would amount to a violation of Article 14; and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 10 of the Vth Schedule of 
the ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them 
for years, with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen.” 


But in the instant matter, Petitioner has failed to adduce any evidence that he was appointed by Respondent by 
following recruitment procedure or he was working against any sanctioned permanent post in the Respondent 
management. Petitioner failed to adduce any evidence on record that the Respondent was indulged in any unfair 
labour practice by not filling the permanent post even though such post was available and by calling to employ 
workman as temporary or daily wages employees despite performing the same work as regular workman on lower 
wages. Therefore, for the want of such plea and evidence, the claim of the Petitioner for regularization in the 
Respondent service is not acceptable. 


Further, in the case of Hari Nandan Prasad v Employer I/R to Management of Food Corporation of India20 
(“FCI”), Hon'ble Supreme Court of India have held: 


“34. On a harmonious reading of the two judgments discussed in detail above, we are of the opinion that when 
there are posts available, in the absence of any unfair labour practice the Labour Court would not give 
direction for regularisation only because a worker has continued as daily- wage worker/ad hoc/temporary 
worker for number of years. Further, if there are no posts available, such a direction for regularization would 
be impermissible. In the aforesaid circumstances giving of direction to regularise such a person, only on the 
basis of number of years put in by such a worker as daily-wager, etc. may amount to back door entry into the 
service which is an anathema to Article 14 of the Constitution. Further, such a direction would not be given 
when the worker concerned does not meet the eligibility requirement of the post in question as per the 
recruitment rules. However, wherever it is found that similarly situated workmen are regularised by the 
employer itself under some scheme or otherwise and the workmen in question who have approached the 
Industrial/Labour Court are on a par with them, direction of regularisation in such cases may be legally 
justified, otherwise, non-regularisation of the left-over workers itself would amount to invidious discrimination 
qua them in such cases and would be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Thus, the industrial adjudicator 
would be achieving the equality by upholding Article 14, rather than violating this constitutional provision.” 


Thus, in view of the fore gone discussion and law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above, the 
claim of the Petitioner for regularization is not tenable. 


Thus, Point No.II is decided against the Petitioner accordingly. 


14. Point No.III: In view of the finding given at Points No. I & II, the Petitioner is not entitled to any relief 
claimed and his petition is found to be baseless, devoid of merit and hence, liable to be dismissed. 


Therefore, Point No.III is decided accordingly. 
AWARD 


The claim of the petitioner Shri U. Sambasiva Rao to set aside his termination order w.e.f 10-12-2002 by 
Respondent Management of Food Corporation of India, Hanuman Junction is dismissed. Petition sans merit stand 
dismissed. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

NOTIFICATION 
New Delhi, the l6th September, 2025 


S.R.O. 35.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution and in 
supersession of the Ministry of Defence, Defence Research and Development Organization, Senior Assistant (Hindi) 
and Assistant (Hindi) Group ‘B’ Posts Recruitment Rules, 20l3 in so far as they relate to the post of Assistant 
(Hindi), except as respects things done or omitted to be done before such supersession, the President hereby makes the 
following rules regulating the method of recruitment for the post of Junior Translation Officer in the Defence 
Research and Development Organisation, Ministry of Defence, namely:- 


[८ Short title and commencement.— (|) These rules may be called the Ministry of Defence, Defence Research 
and Development Organisation, Junior Translation Officer (Group “B’ post) Recruitment Rules, 2025. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Number of post, classification and level in pay matrix.— The number of the said post, its classification 
and level in the pay matrix attached thereto shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to these 
tules. 


3. Method of recruitment, age-limit, qualifications, etc.-The method of recruitment, age-limit, qualifications 
and other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to (3) of the said Schedule. 


4. Disqualification.—No person, — 
(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having a spouse living; or 
(b) who having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 
shall be eligible for appointment to the said post: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal 
law applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so doing, exempt 
any person from the operation of this rule. 


5. Power to relax.— Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do, it 
may, by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing and in consultation with the Union Public Service 
Commission, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any class or category of persons. 


6. Saving.— Nothing in these rules shall affect reservation, relaxation of age-limit and other concessions 
required to be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, the Ex- 
servicemen and other special categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government 
from time to time in this regard.

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour & Employment vide its Order No. L-14011/15/2018-IR(DU) 
dated 27.11.2018 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


Con..2 
The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“Whether the action of the management of Indian Coast Guard, Base Maintenance Unit, Chennai, in 
transferring Sh. P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter to [CGS Mandapam in an non-existing post at ICGS 
Mandapam is legal and justified? If not, to what relief Sh. P.Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter is entitled 
to?” 


As per the claim statement the petitioner is an Indian Coast Guard Civilian Employees Union, registered under the 
Trade Union Act, 1926 was formed primarily to protect the interest of the workmen and for the welfare of the 
employees apart from maintaining harmonious relationship with the Management. It is submitted that there are 60 
civilian workmen in the establishment and most of them are members of the Union, this being the only union

functioning in the establishment to espouse the cause of the workmen. It is submitted that the Union raised an 
Industrial Dispute before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C) by letter dated 21.11.2017 under Section 2(K) of 
the Industrial Dispute Act,1947 over the issue relating to the unfair labour practices adopted by the respondent 
Management. It is submitted that the union was registered on 07.07.2017 vide Regn. No.508/TVR under the Trade 
Unions Act, 1947 and thereafter in the General Body Meeting the office bearers were elected. It is submitted that the 
fact relating to the registration of the union and the list of elected office bearers was communicated to the respondent 
Management by letter No.ICGEU/BMU/01/2017, dated 15.07.2017. 


2. It is submitted that the 1 respondent has framed the “Transfer Policy-Civilian” by letter no.CP/0518 dated 
22.11.2006 and circulated to the Regional Commanders for compliance. Para 4(c) deals with Group ‘B’ ‘C’ ‘D’ 
Non-Gazetted personal, wherein it is clearly stated that postings and transfer of these employees are to be kept at 
absolute minimum level keeping in view the administrative requirement and need for manning the posts at various 
stations. It has also been clearly mentioned that in case of transfers being inescapable, volunteers for the postings or 
transfer will be called. As far as possible only volunteers will be transferred to these vacancies. It has also been 
clearly stated that as far as possible the group ‘C’ and ‘D’ employee should not be transferred over long distance 
and efforts should be made to accommodate them near their choice station to the extent possible. 


3. As per the above, Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was elected as Treasurer of the union. Since the Respondent / 
Management was against the formation of the union, the employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was relieved and directed 
to report for duty at ICGS, Mandapam by letter No.CP/277/17, dated 31.10.2017 


4. The transfer order dated 20.10.2017 was not served on the workman till date. While the petitioner union requested 
that Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj be declared a protected workman, but the Management swiftly reacted by transferring 
Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj and victimized him by adopting unfair labour practice. Hence requested the following relief. 


i) To declare that the transfer order bearing no.1340 dated 20.10.2017 issued by the 37 Respondent 
transferring Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter from Basic Maintenance Unit, Chennai to Indian Coast 
Guard Station, Mandapam is not justified as per the guidelines laid down by the 1“ respondent in the Transfer 
Policy CP/0518 dated 22.11.2006 


ii) And to pass such other award/order as this Hon’ble Central Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour 
Court may deem fit and necessary in the circumstances of the case and thus render justice.

5. The respondent in its reply stated that the Indian Coast Guard Civilian Employees Union has not been recognized 
by the Ministry of Defence, as per CGHA letter WE/0302/Welfare dated 09.10.2019.The transfer order of the three 
(3) civilian personal was promulgated vide CGRHQ(E) letter 1340 dated 20.10.17. Accordingly, the individual was 
relieved from Basic Maintenance Unit, Chennai to report at Indian Coast Guard Station, Madapam as per the 
transfer policy and pleaded that the petition be dismissed as devoid of merit. 


6. The Respondent filed the following documents in support of their contention 


Exhibit No. Date Description 

Ex.M1 18.04.2018 Nature of duties carried out by Indian Coast Guard Base 
Maintenance Unit (Chennai) 

Ex.M2 09.10.2019 Service Association and Welfare in Indian Coast Guard 

Ex.M3 22.11.2006 Transfer Policy - Civilians 


7. Heard both learned counsel and perused the records. The point arised for determination is whether the transfer of 
Shri P. Ayan Aurl Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter as ICGS, Mandapam is an not existing post at ICGS, Mandapam is legal 
and justify? If not, what relief is Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar fitter is entitled to? 


8. The claimant in its claim statement stated that the following points regarding the transfer policy. 


(a) Posting and transfer are to be kept at the absolute minimum level 
(b) Volunteers for the postings of the transfer called and will be transferred 
(c) Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ employees should not be transferred over long distance 


9. In petition claim the hardships caused to transferring described as under 


(a) Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was transferred during October,2017 quite impossible for getting admission for his 
school going children at the new station 

(b) The workman unable to shift his family in the midst of the academic year 

(c) The employee kept the family in Chennai for his child to complete the studies in the academic year but the 
Estate Office, CPWD directed him to vacate the quarters and threatened to impose a penalty 

(d) The employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj fell sick because of the mental agony and remains on leave on medical 
ground from 1.11.2017 to 28.6.2018 

(e) When the workman reported for duty on 29.06.2018 at the Mandapam station, the 31 Respondent directed 


him to report for duty in Chennai for four days in a week. 


10. On perusal of whole the claim statement, the claimant nowhere stated that Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was transferred 
to a non-existing post at ICGS Mandapam. On perusal of the claim statement, it appears that the Respondent did not 
violate the transfer policy, as the Mandapam station is not far away from Chennai station. 


11. It is the fundamental duty of transferring employee to seek the permission to overstay at Govt. accommodation by 
mentioning the sufficient reasons for occupation of the allotted house. In claim petition this facts nowhere mention 
that any application mentioning sufficient reasons for over staying at the allotted house was made or not. In this 
situation it can be presumed that no application was made by the transferring employee to the authority. 
Transferring employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj fails to submit the medical certificates which might have established 
the genuine grounds of his absence due to medical reasons. 


12. It is stated in the claim petition that the employee was transferred due to his involvement in the union, but the 
claimant fails to submit any evidence that may establish this fact that respondent had showed its jealous against the 
employee. The only vague reason given is that he was an elected as an office bearer in the union, the transfer of an 
employee do not appear as a result of his election to the union. 


13. The claimant has stated that no transfer order was provided to the transferred employee and that only a relieving 
order was provided to the transferee employee. The relieving order issued to Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj dated 
31.10.2017 is available at page no.2 of the paper book in this document, it is mentioned clearly that the Competent 
Authority has approved the transfer of Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj with a direction to report at ICGS Mandapam by 
10.11.2017. The relieving order was issued by the Section Officer in compliance with the order passed by the 
Competent Authority hence, no right of the transfree employee was violated by not providing a separate transfer 
order.

favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.”

by or on behalf of the workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In 
such a situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead 
evidence to establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, 
who would fail if no evidence is led.”’

Further it has been pleaded by the respondent in their written statement as under:-

b). The Learned Regional Labour Commissioner, Lucknow, without proper application of mind, contrary to the

c). As per the provisions of section 2 A sub section (3), of the Industrial Disputes’ Act, 1947, any application for 
adjudicating any dispute or difference between a workman and his employer connected with, or arising out of

discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination shall be made to the Labour Court or Tribunal before the expiry of 
three years from the date of such discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination. 


d). A limitation of three years for raising an industrial dispute has been provided in the Industrial Disputes' Act, 1947,

On behalf of respondent evidence on affidavit of Shri Ashotosh Anand, Chief Manager, HRM of the bank filed, he 
was cross examined on 04.05.2015. 


On behalf of workman on 27.06.2016 rejoinder affidavit has been filed denying the averments as taken by respondent. 


On 05.11.2020, workman/claimant has filed evidence on affidavit (Examination in Chief) and he was cross examined 
on 07.01.2021, by respondent. 


During the pendency of case as per notification dated 26.11.2019, moved by the Ministry Of Finance (Department of 
Financial Services), relevant portion quoted herein below:- 


Baroda Uttar Pradesh Gramin Bank, Kashi Gomti Samyut Gramin Bank and Purvanchal Bank (hereinafter 
referred to as "the transferor Regional Rural Banks") sponsored by the Bank of Baroda, Union Bank of India 
and State Bank of India in the State of Uttar Pradesh are hereby amalgamated into a single Regional Rural 
Bank which shall be called as Baroda U.P. Bank (hereinafter referred to as "the transferee Regional Rural 
Bank") with its head office at Gorakhpur under the sponsorship of Bank of Baroda. 


Accordingly as per the said notification respondent 10.1 0 & 1B were imp leaded as party, In view of the law laid 
down by Hon’ble Madras High Court in case of Palanisamy R vs. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, 2001 
LawSuit(Mad) 152, and also in the case of Shri Kanchi Kamakoti Peetam Charitable Trust Hospital vs. Industrial 
Tribunal & Others, 2004 (100) FLR 1166. 


I have heard Shri Parvez Alam legal representative of claimant, and Shri Adarsh Jagdhari learned counsel for 
respondent. 


After hearing the parties/their legal representative and Advocate, the first point to be considered the point to be 
consider in the present case:- 


A). whether the reference dated 17.02.2015, is vague and on the basis of the same no cause of action arises on the 
part of workman/claimant to file present claim petition. 


In order to decide the said dispute it would be appropriate to go through Section 10 of the Industrial Dispute Act. 
10. Section 10 of Industrial Disputes Act reads thus: 


"10. Reference of disputes to Boards, Courts or Tribunals. (1) [Where the appropriate Government is of 
opinion that any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended, it may at any time), by order in writing,- 


(a) refer the dispute to a Board for promoting a settlement thereof; or 
(b) refer any matter appearing to be connected with or relevant to the dispute to a Court for inquiry; or 


[(c) refer the dispute or any matter appearing to be connected with, or relevant to, the dispute, if it relates to 
any matter specified in the Second Schedule, to a Labour Court for adjudication; or 


(d) refer the dispute or any matter appearing to be connected with, or relevant to, the dispute, whether it 
relates to any matter specified in the Second Schedule or the Third Schedule, to a Tribunal for adjudication: 


Provided that where the dispute relates to any matter specified in the Third Schedule and is not likely to 
affect more than one hundred workmen, the appropriate Government may, if it so thinks fit, make the 
reference to a Labour Court under clause (c):]" 


11. Plain reading of aforesaid provision would show that when industrial dispute exists or is apprehended, appropriate 
Government can refer dispute to Court for enquiry or if relates to any matter specified in Second Schedule to Labour 
Court for adjudication or make Reference to Tribunal, if dispute relates to matters specified in Second Schedule or 
Third Schedule. It is, therefore, obvious that Reference can be made only when industrial disputes exists or is 
apprehended by Competent Authority. 


13. The aforesaid legal position would make explicit that existence of industrial dispute is a paramount and important 
consideration while dealing with Reference. 


Only existent or apprehended industrial disputes can be referred for consideration of Court or Tribunal. However, at 
the time of taking decision whether Reference to be made or not, appropriate Government need not venture into 


4068 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 9, 2026/VAISAKHA 19, 1948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


merits of dispute, as making Reference is only administrative function. Only because Reference is made under 
Section 10(1), Court or Tribunal is not precluded from entering into aspects of delay and laches or to record findings 
as to existence or non-existence of dispute. 


In case of Prabhakar v. Joint Director, Sericulture Department and "another, 2015 (147) FLR 341 (SC), the 
Hon’ble Supreme Court considered and held the impact of delay and laches in Reference made under Section 10(1) of 
Industrial Disputes Act and observed in paragraph No. 14 as under: 


"40. An industrial dispute has to be referred by the appropriate Government for adjudication and the 
workman cannot approach the Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal directly, except in those cases which are 
covered by Section 2-A of the Act. Reference is made under Section 10 of the Act in those cases where the 
appropriate Government forms an opinion that ‘any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended’. The words 
‘industrial dispute exists' are of paramount importance unless there is an existence of an industrial dispute 
(or the dispute is apprehended or it is apprehended such a dispute may arise in near future), no reference is 
to be made. Thus, existence or apprehension of an industrial dispute is a sine qua non for making the 
reference. No doubt, at the time of taking a decision whether a reference is to be made or not, the 
appropriate Government is not to go into the merits of the dispute. Making of reference is only an 
administrative function. At the same time, on the basis of material on record, satisfaction of the existence of 
the industrial dispute or the apprehension of an industrial dispute is necessary. Such existence/apprehension 
of industrial dispute, thus, becomes a condition precedent, though it will be only subjective satisfaction 
based on material on record. Since, we are not concerned with the satisfaction dealing with cases where 
there is apprehended industrial dispute, discussion that follows would confine to existence of an industrial 
dispute. Dispute or difference arises when one party make a demand and other party rejects the same. It is 
held by this Court in number of cases that before raising the industrial dispute making of demand is a 
necessary pre-condition. In such a scenario, if the services of a workman are terminated and he does not 
make the demand and/or raise the issue alleging wrongful termination immediately thereafter or within 
reasonable time and raises the same after considerable lapse of period, whether it can be said that industrial 
dispute still exist. Since there is no period of limitation, it gives right to the workman to raise the dispute 
even belatedly. However, if the dispute is raised after a long period, it has to be seen as to whether such a 
dispute still exists? Thus, notwithstanding the fact that law of limitation does not apply, it is to be shown by 
the workman that there is a dispute in praesenti. For this purpose, he has to demonstrate that even if 
considerable period has lapsed and there are laches and delays, such delay has not resulted into making the 
industrial dispute seized to exist. Therefore, if the workman is able to give satisfactory explanation for these 
laches and delays and demonstrate that the circumstances discloses that issue is still alive, delay would not 
come in his way because of the reason that law of limitation has no application. On the other hand, if 
because of such delay dispute no longer remains alive and is to be treated as "dead", then it would be non- 
existent dispute which cannot be referred." 


Thus it can be held on the point in issue that for raising industrial dispute demand is precondition. In case, employee 
fails to make demand, dispute cannot be referred. 


From the perusal of claim statement filed by claimant on 06.05.2005, undisputed facts which emerged out that he was 
initially appointed as casual labour on the post of jamadaar cum chaprasi in the purvanchal gramin bank, Gorakhpur, 
now known as Baroda UP bank, in the branch saleempur dewaria, in the said capacity he worked and discharged his 
duties up till 29.04.2006, his services were retrenched/terminated, so workman raise a Industrial Dispute and by

By order No. K-10/2/2022-IR dated 21.10.2022 the present industrial dispute has been referred for 
adjudication to this Tribunal in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2A) 
of Section 10 the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947) by the Central Government, with following schedule: 


"Whether the action of the management of North Eastern Railway, Gorakhpur and Lucknow in terminating 
the services of Shri Krishna Chandra Dwivedi, Casual Labour w.e.f. 31.12.1976 is justified and legal? If not 
to what relief the workman is entitled to” 


Accordingly, an industrial dispute No. 12/2024 has been registered on 24.04.2024. 


From the perusal of record, the position which emerge out is that the till date the claimant/workman has not filed any 
statement of claim in spite of repeated opportunity given to him, in order to establish his claim, as per the reference 
dated 21.10.2022. 


So in view of the said facts, as well as the law laid by the Hon’ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. 
Labour Court (I) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


“Tt is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality 
of the order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a 
workman raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file 
written statement before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must 
also produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce 
evidence, the dispute referred by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he 
would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (I), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. 
Raj Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) FLR 38 
and Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on 
behalf of the workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a 
situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to 
establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail 
if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. A 
perusal of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led by the 
respondent. In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.” 


As the workman has not filed any statement of claim/oral/documentary evidence, so the present case is liable to be 
dismissed. 


For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and; and the workman is not entitled for any relief. 
Award as above.

In July 2018, the answering respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and 
M/s Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e-tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide 
conservancy services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no. 2 
submits bill for payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed their duties and answering respondent is 
only responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command Chandigarh to release payment directly to 
the contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is

1. Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against his termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along with 
continuity of service and full back wages. 


2. It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that he was appointed as sweeper/safai karamchari 
on 01.09.2012 by respondent no.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But the said minimum 
wages were never paid to him. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 1.75% ESI and Rs.300/- as 
TDS from hissalary despite of the fact that his total wages comes under the ambit of taxfree limit. He was working 
under respondent 10.1 directly, but respondent 10.1 in order to avoid its liability always shows his employment in 
record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


3. It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent 10.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent no.1. However, their demand was not accepted. 
Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently his services were dispensed with w.e.f. 
27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent 10.1 retained juniors in service and also made fresh appointments 
after termination of his services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of the Act. Thus, there is violation 
of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4. Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


5. Respondent no.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to the 
Court with clean hands as he was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage rate as 
prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non-Cantonment 
Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering respondent entered into 
contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). In July 2018, the answering 
respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and M/s Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e- 
tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide conservancy services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for 
the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed 
their duties and answering respondent is only responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command 
Chandigarh to release payment directly to the contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. 
Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent 
has no responsibility of disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai 
karamcharis formed union in the headquarter, which is not permitted and also carried out demonstration inside the 
premises of Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent 
asked respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility 
for termination services of the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the answering 
respondent and the workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the answering 
respondent cannot organize themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative office of the 
Government of India. In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union unauthorizedly and 
indulge in unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor and therefore, termination 
is the prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed.

6. Respondent no.2 also filed reply maintaining therein that workman worked with it w.e.f. 05.07.2018 to 
27.10.2018. Respondent no.2 has not terminated the services of workman. Workman was paid minimum wages as 
declared by the Centre Government from time to time. Workman himself left the job at his own will without notice. It 
is prayed that the claim may be dismissed.

7. In order to prove his case, workman examined himself as WW1 and tendered into evidence his affidavit 
WWIH/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent 10.1. AR for workman closed the evidence on

Submissions of workman:- 


10. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by respondent 
10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent 10.2. The workman was appointed directly by respondent no.1 
on 01.09.2012 as sweeper and his services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any reason in violation of 
Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and junior to him were retained in 
service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So far as the agreements between the 
respondent 10.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair labour practice. The work performed by 
the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having any license. The contractor has left after three
